engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening: Italian Game Basics
chess.body: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. White targets f7, the weakest square in Black's position. Giuoco Piano (3...Bc5) leads to rich middlegame. Learn: castle early, play d3, develop bishop to e3, then push d4 for centre control. Safe, instructive, good for learning. Magnus Carlsen played this at the top level.

wisdom.title: Being a Better Husband
wisdom.body: The best fathers are also good partners. Your daughter watches how you treat her mother. That becomes her template for relationships. Simple acts: say thank you. Notice when your partner is tired. Take something off her plate without being asked. Ask about her day and actually listen. Small but it compounds.

book.author: Tim Ferriss
book.chapter: The 80/20 of Everything: Most Effort Is Wasted
book.lesson: Ferriss's most useful contribution: ruthless application of Pareto's 80/20 principle to everything. 20% of customers generate 80% of revenue — and usually 120% of headaches. 20% of tasks generate 80% of results. 20% of foods cause 80% of health problems for a given person. The exercise: list every customer, task, and activity. Identify the 20% producing 80% of value. Do more of that. Then identify the 20% consuming 80% of your time and energy with minimal value. Eliminate, automate, or delegate it. Most knowledge workers are busy with the bottom 80% and neglect the top 20%.
book.key_quote: Being busy is not the same as being productive. Most of what we do doesn't matter nearly as much as we think it does.
book.action: List your 10 most frequent work activities. Rank by impact. The bottom 3 — can any be eliminated, automated, or delegated?
crux: The New Rich optimise for time and mobility, not for accumulation then retirement.
Deferred-life planning is the default and it is a bad plan.
Dreamlining: cost out the specific life you want. It is usually cheaper than assumed.
Relative income (per hour) beats absolute income.
Pareto: 80% of results come from 20% of inputs. Find and cut the rest.
Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time available. Short deadlines force focus.
Use both together — do only the important, and give it very little time.
Selective ignorance: a low-information diet is a productivity intervention.
Batch everything. Email, calls, errands. Context switching is the tax.
Automate with clear rules and delegated authority, or you've just added coordination work.
Build a muse: a product with recurring revenue that doesn't need your presence.
Test demand before building anything. Cheap ads before inventory.
Mini-retirements beat one long retirement at the end.
Fear-setting: define the worst case in detail and it usually shrinks.
learnings: Being busy is often a form of avoidance.
Cutting the wrong work beats optimising it.
Deadlines are a focus tool, not just a commitment.
Automation without decision rules just moves the work.
examples: Ferriss cut 98% of his client list, kept the top 5, and income rose while hours dropped from 80 to 15.
BrainQUICKEN was validated with small Google Ads spends before stock was ordered.
Fear-setting a trip to London: worst case listed, all reversible. He went.
adapt: The bots are the muse infrastructure — they run whether you're interviewing or asleep.
80/20 the content: which posts actually drive followers? Cut the rest.
Batch Telegram and email into two windows. This is the same fix Deep Work prescribes.
Fear-set the Dubai move: worst case is a return to KL with more experience. Reversible.

minimalism.title: Space Is A Feature
minimalism.body: Empty space in a room is not wasted space, the same way white space on a page is not wasted paper. Both exist so the things that matter can be seen.
minimalism.action: Remove one item from your most crowded shelf. Add nothing back.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Remember The Detail
etiquette.body: Their daughter's exam. Their father's surgery. Ask next time. This is the single highest-return social habit and almost nobody keeps notes.
etiquette.action: Write down one personal detail after your next conversation.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Enough Is A Number
stillness.body: Without a defined 'enough', more is the only direction and the target moves with every increment. AED 30K/month is a number. Undefined ambition is not a goal, it is a treadmill.
stillness.action: Write your 'enough' figure. Date it. Revisit in a year.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Circle Of Competence
model.body: The boundary matters more than the size. Knowing precisely where your knowledge ends is worth more than extending it slightly. Most large losses happen just outside the edge.
model.action: Draw your circle. Name one thing just outside it you have been treating as inside.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: Say it plainly. Pretending to know is worse in every culture, and obvious in all of them.
arabic.label: Arabic

drill.title: Number Sense: Orders Of Magnitude
drill.body: Is that number plausible? A company with 200 staff and AED 4bn revenue implies AED 20m per head — almost certainly wrong. This check catches more errors than any other.
drill.action: Sanity-check five figures by per-unit magnitude.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Walking Is Underrated
health.body: 8,000 steps a day is associated with a large mortality reduction versus 4,000, and the curve is steepest at the low end. The gains come from moving more, not from moving harder.
health.action: Add one 15-minute walk. After a meal is best for glucose.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Warren Buffett
quote.quote: Rule No.1: Never lose money. Rule No.2: Never forget Rule No.1.

lesson.lesson: Beware the barrenness of a busy life.

case.title: Flipkart vs Amazon India
case.story: Flipkart was winning India. Then Amazon entered with $5B, same-day delivery, and superior tech. Walmart bought Flipkart for $16B — a defensive acquisition.
case.lesson: Speed of execution beats being first. Amazon wasn't first in India, but they executed faster. Being early means nothing if you don't keep innovating.

fpna.title: Variance Analysis
fpna.body: Volume variance + Price/Rate variance + Mix variance = Total variance. Always decompose before presenting.

cfo.title: CFO Step 5: Culture + People
cfo.body: The best CFOs build finance teams that the business trusts. Hire people better than you. Create a learning culture. A CFO who hoards information creates a bottleneck. One who shares insight creates leverage.

money_hack.title: Auto-Sweep FD
money_hack.body: Link savings to sweep FD. Idle cash earns FD rates automatically.

dubai.title: Free zone vs mainland, in one line
dubai.body: A free-zone entity is 100% foreign-owned, tax-advantaged and restricted to trading within its zone or abroad. A mainland entity can trade anywhere in the UAE and pays the 9%. Groups run both, and the intercompany between them is where the FP&A work lives.
dubai.targets: If you can explain this cleanly, you are ahead of most candidates.
dubai.action: Practise the explanation in 30 seconds. It comes up constantly.

desk.productivity: Read 10 pages of non-fiction daily. 10 × 365 = 12 books/year.

father.title: Get down on the floor
father.do: Ten minutes of tummy-adjacent floor time where you are lying at her eye level, not looming above.
father.why: Physical perspective changes the interaction from supervision to companionship. It also builds the core strength that precedes crawling and sitting unsupported.

father.title: Name the feeling, not the behaviour
father.do: When she cries, say what she is feeling: 'you are tired' or 'that frightened you.'
father.why: She cannot parse it yet. You are building the habit in yourself — parents who label emotions early keep doing it at three and at thirteen, which is when it matters.

life_wisdom.teaching: Every claim is true only under stated conditions. Jain logic prefixes assertions with 'in some respect' to keep the conditions visible.
life_wisdom.apply: Attach the assumption to the forecast, out loud: 'growth is 12% — in the respect that the two new stores open in Q3.' Half of forecasting disputes are actually undeclared conditions.

life_wisdom.teaching: The test has four parts, and speech must pass all of them. True but cruel fails. True and kind but badly timed also fails.
life_wisdom.apply: Before delivering hard feedback, run all four. Most feedback that lands badly is true and useful but fails on timing.

vocab.note: Names the real consequence of a decision people are framing as minor.

speaking.title: Lose the apology
speaking.drill: Speak for two minutes without 'sorry', 'just', or 'I might be wrong but'.
speaking.why: Hedging language before a fact invites challenge to the fact. Reserve qualifiers for genuine uncertainty.

interview_tech.q: What is your WACC and how would you set the hurdle rate for a new store?
interview_tech.a: WACC = cost of equity × equity weight + after-tax cost of debt × debt weight. Cost of equity via CAPM: risk-free rate plus beta times equity risk premium, with a country risk premium for emerging markets. But do not use group WACC as the store hurdle — a new store in a new market is riskier than the average of the existing business. Add a premium and be explicit about it. The common error is a single group hurdle applied to everything, which systematically over-invests in risky projects and under-invests in safe ones.

interview_tech.q: Your ERP implementation is running three months late. What do you tell the steering committee?
interview_tech.a: The date, the cause, the options with costs, and your recommendation. Be specific about which workstream is late and why — usually data migration or the volume of unresolved customisation requests, not the software. Present the real choice: go live late and clean, or on time with manual workarounds and a defined remediation plan. Quantify the workaround cost in FTE months. Having led D365 across two countries, the credible line is that data quality determines the date more than configuration does.

interview_soft.q: The board pushes back hard on your numbers in front of everyone. What do you do?
interview_soft.a: Do not defend and do not fold. Separate the challenge into fact and judgement. If they have spotted a factual error, concede immediately and precisely — 'you are right, that is the restated base, I will recirculate by Thursday.' Credibility survives errors; it does not survive defensiveness. If it is a judgement call, state your assumption, the sensitivity, and offer the alternative case. Never argue methodology in the room; take it offline with the one director who raised it.

interview_soft.q: An employee asks you to approve an expense that is within policy but clearly wrong. What now?
interview_soft.a: They are testing whether you hide behind rules. Policy is a floor, not a ceiling. Approve or reject on the substance, explain the reasoning to the person directly, and then fix the policy so the next person is not in the same position. If it involves a senior person, the answer does not change — that is precisely when it counts. Say plainly that you would escalate to the audit committee if pressured to approve something you believe is wrong.
interview_soft.who: Any group with a code of conduct
